full_judgment:
18. Dr. Rahman while arguing the case tried to impress upon me that if the decree of the learned trial court is maintained it would not in any way affect the registered deed dated 8.1.83 nor the record of right with regard to .40V2 decimals of Land which admittedly stands in the name of the defendants. If that remain intact a member of the public may be misguided by those documents in the future and in fact a bonafide purchaser from the defendants on the strength of those two documents may suffer and that may also give rise to multiplicity of the suits and therefore relying on section 54 of sub-section (e) of the Specific Relief Act he submits that the instant suit is barred under the aforesaid section. As against that Mr. Saha submitted that section 54 of sub-section (e) supports him and not the defendants because this sub-section postulates that in an appropriate case the court would grant injunction in the form of permanent injunction to prevent multiciplity of suits. Multiplicity of judicial proceedings may result, for example, from recurring violations of plaintiffs right. It is not necessary to lead positive evidence to show that the defendant intends to invade the right in the future also. The question can be determined on the probability of the case. In the instant case there is positive assertions from the side of the plaintiff that the defendant already threatened him to dispossess on 16.4.83 and the possibility of dispossessing the plaintiff from the suit land will remain there until an injunction is granted. Mr. Saha further submitted that if the decree of the learned trial court is not maintained, rather that would give rise to multiciplity of suits as in the absence of the decree the defendants on the strength of the deed dated 8.3.83 would dispossess the plaintiff from the suit plot and then he will have to go to the court for filing another suit for declaration of title and recovery of possession and the plaintiff will have to file a suit for correction of record of right and, may be, for cancellation of the deed dated 8.3.83. There is another aspect of the case in that possession is prima fade proof of ownership. Possession of property, movable or immovable, affords prima fade presumption of ownership as man generally own the property they possess. Possession is title against anyone who cannot prove a better hue. So, a prospective buyer of the suit land infuture cannot be misled by those two documents when he will find the plaintiff in possession. So, I find substance in the submission of Mr. Saha that section 54(e) helps him in this case. 

 19. Now I would like to consider the legal aspect of the case. It appears from the trend of the earlier judicial pronouncements that in a suit for permanent injunction the plaintiff is to prove exclusive, possession of the suit land and incidentally a prima fade title to the suit land. If these two requirements are fulfilled by the plaintiff, only then he is entitled to get a permanent injunction. If we look to section 110 of the Evidence Act we find that this section embodies the well known principle of Roman Law that possession is prima facie proof of owner ship and when, therefore, a person is in possession of a property the presumption of ownership is highly in his favour and under s 110 the onus of proving that he is not the owner is on the person who asserts that he is not the owner.
